        <span class="abstract__title">PLEASE UPLOAD YOUR SLIDES: What does it take to render Pixi-perfect PDFs in CI?!</span>

        <span class="abstract__when">Wednesday, October 21 · <time datetime="2026-10-21T15:15:00-07:00">3:15</time>–<time datetime="2026-10-21T16:30:00-07:00">4:30pm</time> · San Jose Ballroom Salon 3 &amp; 4</span>

    <div class="abstract__body">{% capture abstract_md %}Software which promises to let you write slides or docs as code often delivers excellent experiences when rendered to HTML, in exchange for some tedium in codifying layouts in plain-text. In this RAM talk I contend that the ecosystem for reproducibly generating Latex PDFs of docs or slides is still missing out on some of the "it just works" feeling that web-native content workflows seem to have.{% endcapture %}{{ abstract_md | markdownify }}<p class="abstract__meta"><a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583" target="_blank" rel="noopener">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583</a></p></div>

        <span class="abstract__when">Wednesday, October 21 · <time datetime="2026-10-21T15:15:00-07:00">3:15</time>–<time datetime="2026-10-21T16:30:00-07:00">4:30pm</time> · San Jose Ballroom Salon 3 &amp; 4</span>

      <h2 class="abstract__heading" id="dogs-design-why-caring-for-a-reactive-dog-is-like-creating-user-centered-software">
        <span class="abstract__title">Dogs &amp; design: why caring for a reactive dog is like creating user-centered software</span>
        <span class="abstract__people">Kate Arneson</span>
        <span class="abstract__when">Wednesday, October 21 · <time datetime="2026-10-21T15:15:00-07:00">3:15</time>–<time datetime="2026-10-21T16:30:00-07:00">4:30pm</time> · San Jose Ballroom Salon 3 &amp; 4</span>
      </h2>
    </summary>
    <div class="abstract__body">{% capture abstract_md %}Caring for a dog may not be human-centered, but it is user-centered. I'll share what my reactive and anxious dog has taught me about challenging assumptions, engaging community, and meeting users where they're at — dogs and humans alike.{% endcapture %}{{ abstract_md | markdownify }}<p class="abstract__meta"><a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583" target="_blank" rel="noopener">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583</a></p></div>

  <details class="abstract">
    <summary class="abstract__summary">
      <h2 class="abstract__heading" id="on-trust-adopting-autonomous-software-factories-in-rse-organizations">
        <span class="abstract__title">On Trust: Adopting Autonomous Software Factories in RSE Organizations</span>
        <span class="abstract__people">Geoffrey Lentner and Chimdia Kabuo</span>
        <span class="abstract__when">Wednesday, October 21 · <time datetime="2026-10-21T15:15:00-07:00">3:15</time>–<time datetime="2026-10-21T16:30:00-07:00">4:30pm</time> · San Jose Ballroom Salon 3 &amp; 4</span>
      </h2>
    </summary>
    <div class="abstract__body">{% capture abstract_md %}Coding agents have divided the research software engineering community. RSEs who value the craft of writing code tend to resist them, and those who mostly want what the code produces tend to welcome them. Both camps frame trust as a question of authorship (who wrote the code, and whether anyone read it). That framing does not scale to an autonomous software factory, in which agents plan, write, test, and review code from a specification faster than people can read it.

Computing and science already depend on tools their users did not build and do not inspect. Few programmers read the assembly their compilers emit, and astronomers do not grind their own telescope mirrors; in both cases trust rests on calibration, testing, and reproducibility. We argue that a software factory is an instrument of the same kind, sitting between the RSE and the code. Agent-written scientific code can then earn trust on its merits rather than on who wrote it, and the argument asks no one to take a model's output on faith. Those merits are measurable, through validation against problems with known answers, deterministic simulation testing (which replays any failure from the seed that produced it), and independent reruns that reproduce the result. Within an organization that adopts a factory, the RSE works as its instrument scientist (specifying it, calibrating it, and deciding when its output is fit for use).{% endcapture %}{{ abstract_md | markdownify }}<p class="abstract__meta"><a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583" target="_blank" rel="noopener">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583</a></p></div>
  </details>

  <details class="abstract">
    <summary class="abstract__summary">
      <h2 class="abstract__heading" id="we-were-warned-about-this-ai-futurism-in-media">
        <span class="abstract__title">We were warned about this! AI futurism in media</span>
        <span class="abstract__people">Tinashe M. Tapera</span>
        <span class="abstract__when">Wednesday, October 21 · <time datetime="2026-10-21T15:15:00-07:00">3:15</time>–<time datetime="2026-10-21T16:30:00-07:00">4:30pm</time> · San Jose Ballroom Salon 3 &amp; 4</span>
      </h2>
    </summary>
    <div class="abstract__body">{% capture abstract_md %}As technologists, programmers, and research software engineers, we often look to scientific and engineering-oriented literature to predict how artificial intelligence will change our work, our relationships, and our society; but the fields of literature, film, and television offer several well-reasoned opinions and predictions in the futurism genre. In this presentation, we examine some unexpected examples of futurism in fictional literature, film, and television to find out what there is to learn about science, technology, and society in the age of AI{% endcapture %}{{ abstract_md | markdownify }}<p class="abstract__meta"><a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583" target="_blank" rel="noopener">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23353583</a></p></div>
  </details>
